lessonRef.focus: repairing responses whose evidence does not match the claim
lessonRef.title: Reteach and varied practice: repairing responses whose evidence does not match the claim

studentTask.text: This Grade 4 lesson develops repairing responses whose evidence does not match the claim within the unit “An Evidence Habit: Details, Examples, and Inferences.” Read the delivered Academy-original source before responding. Strong ELA work separates what the source explicitly says from what a reader infers, selects evidence because it is relevant and sufficient, and explains the connection instead of leaving a quotation to speak for itself. Today's reteach and varied practice work asks you to make that reasoning visible and to revise if the evidence does not support the first idea.

sourceReference.text:
The snow fence along the north field had blown down every winter for as long as anyone could remember, and every spring Grandpa Elias rebuilt it stronger.

He used heavier posts one year. The wind took them. He used deeper post holes the next year. The wind took those too, tearing the slats apart and scattering them into the ditch like spilled matchsticks.

June was eleven the winter she started keeping notes. She wrote down the direction of the storms, which was almost always northwest, and where the fence broke first, which was almost always the same forty-foot stretch near the low spot. She wrote down something else: the fence never broke where the old lilac hedge stood beside it.

"The hedge holds it," she told her grandfather.

"The hedge is a windbreak," he said. "A fence is not a hedge."

"No," June said. "The hedge moves."

He stopped stacking slats and looked at her.

That spring they rebuilt the forty-foot stretch differently. They set the posts no deeper than before, but they left the slats loose at one end, so the whole panel could give a little and swing back. Grandpa Elias called it sloppy work three separate times while he was doing it.

The first storm came in November, hard out of the northwest. June stood at the kitchen window and watched the loose section shudder, lean, and rock back upright. In the morning it was still standing. The tight, strong, properly built section forty feet to the east lay flat in the snow.

Grandpa Elias walked the fence line twice without saying anything. Then he came in, poured coffee, and set his hat on the table.

"Fifty years," he said, "I have been building it to win."

June waited.

"A thing that will not move," he said, "is just waiting to break."

guidedSupport.text:
Use this source-specific routine for “The Fence That Learned to Bend”:
1. Preview the title and paragraph structure; write what repairing responses whose evidence does not match the claim asks you to notice or do.
2. Mark one statement the source makes explicitly and one inference a reader could draw. Keep the two kinds of thinking separate.
3. Test the inference with the evidence requirement in today's task. If the evidence is weak or incomplete, narrow or revise the inference.
4. Draft your own response. A facilitator may clarify directions or ask questions, but may not supply your claim, evidence choice, sentences, or revision.

independentEvidenceTask.text:
Read “The Fence That Learned to Bend,” then answer: Identify one earlier misunderstanding about repairing responses whose evidence does not match the claim. Use this reading to correct it and explain why the correction is stronger.

Deliverable: Grade 4: a before-and-after correction supported by the source; write one organized paragraph.

Evidence requirement: Use two exact details. Label source evidence with a paragraph number or another precise location. Your response must explain the connection between the evidence and your conclusion.

remediation.text:
If repairing responses whose evidence does not match the claim is not yet secure, return to “The Fence That Learned to Bend” before starting over:
- Evidence gap: underline the exact words that support the idea and label their paragraph or location.
- Reasoning gap: complete the stem “This evidence matters because …” in your own words, then reread the question.
- Overclaim: name what the source does not establish and narrow the conclusion to what the evidence can support.
- Completion gap: compare the draft with each learner success criterion and repair one missing part at a time.

extension.text: Apply repairing responses whose evidence does not match the claim to a different paragraph or a defensible alternative interpretation of “The Fence That Learned to Bend.” Compare the new result with your first response and explain which evidence changes, which reasoning still holds, and why.
